paragraphs.source_en: Just then, unexpectedly, Kangetsu came in, saying, "I beg your pardon for having troubled you the other day." "Ah, Kangetsu, it has been a long time. I have just been listening to a splendid piece of prose, and it has driven away the lingering spirit of my 'Tochimenbo.'" Mr. Meitei let fall a few words that made no sense at all. "Is that so? I see." Kangetsu too replied with an equally senseless greeting. Only the master showed no particular sign of being in high spirits. He said, "The man you introduced the other day, Ochi Kochi, came here." Kangetsu said, "Oh, did he come? That fellow Ochi Kochi is an exceedingly honest man, but he is a little peculiar, so I was afraid he might trouble you; still, he insisted that I introduce him, and so..." The master said, "There was no particular trouble." "When he came to your house, did he say anything about his name?" The master said, "No, I do not think he said anything of the sort." Kangetsu said, "Is that so? He has a habit of explaining his name to everyone he meets for the first time, wherever he goes." Meitei, who was always waiting for some fresh amusement, at once broke in and asked, "What sort of explanation does he give?" "He is terribly bothered if people read the name Tofu by its Chinese-style pronunciation..." "Well now, that is strange." As he said this, Mr. Meitei pinched out a little tobacco from his leather pouch patterned with gold brocade. Mr. Kangetsu said, "He always makes a point of saying, 'My name is not Ochi Tofu; it is Ochi Kochi.'" "How amusing!" Meitei drew the smoke from his Kumoi tobacco deep down into his belly. Kangetsu said, "It comes entirely from his passion for literature. If Tofu is read as Kochi, then joined to his family name it becomes Ochikochi, sounding the same as the idiom 'far and near.' Not only that, but the four syllables also rhyme, and he is extremely proud of it. That is why he is always complaining that if people read his Tofu by the Chinese reading, all the pains he has taken go completely unappreciated." When Mr. Meitei heard this, he said, "Indeed, that certainly is rather unusual." This excited Mr. Meitei's interest all the more; he blew the Kumoi smoke he had drawn into his belly back toward his nostrils, and midway the smoke could find no outlet and caught in his throat. The gentleman clutched his pipe stem and began coughing, "ahem, ahem." The master also said with a laugh, "When he came the other day, he said he played the boatman at a recitation meeting and was laughed at by the schoolgirls." Meitei swung up his pipe and struck his kneecap with it. "Yes, exactly, exactly. How amusing!" Feeling that it was dangerous to stay too close to him, I quickly moved a little away. Meitei went on, "That very recitation meeting. He mentioned it to me the other day when I treated him to Tochimenbo.

paragraphs.source_zh: 就在这时，想不到寒月君口称“上次多有打搅”，走了进来。“啊，寒月君，久违久违，现在我正在拜听一篇了不起的好文章，把我的‘橡面坊’的阴魂给驱散了哩。”迷亭先生说了几句无头无脑的话。“是吗，原来是这样啊？”寒月也回答了一句无头无脑的话。唯独主人并不显得怎样兴高采烈。他说：“前几天你介绍的那个叫越智东风的人来了。”寒月说：“他来了吗？这个叫越智东风的，倒是个非常老实的人，不过多少有点怪，我本来怕给您添麻烦，可他非让我把他介绍给您不可，所以……”主人道：“倒也没有什么麻烦。”“他到府上来，有没有讲有关他的姓名的事儿？”主人道：“不，好像没有讲什么。”寒月道：“是吗？他有个毛病，无论到哪儿去，总要向第一次会面的人解释一番他的名字。”迷亭是个巴不得找点什么新鲜事儿的人，立刻插嘴问道：“怎么个讲解法儿呀？”“他唯恐别人用汉字音来读他那个东风的名字……”“这倒奇啦。”迷亭先生说着，从他那绘有泥金花纹的皮制烟荷包里捏出一点烟丝来。寒月先生说：“他总是告诉人家说：‘我的名字不读做Ochitofu，而是Ochikochi’哩。”“真有意思！”迷亭把云井牌烟丝冒出来的烟一直深深吸进肚里。寒月道：“这完全是出于对文学的着迷，如果念成Kochi，那么和姓连在一起就成了Ochikochi，就和成语‘远近’同音。不但这样，而且这四个音节又都合辙押韵，他对这点非常得意哩。所以他常发牢骚说：如果用汉音去读我这个东风，那么我的一番苦心就给白白糟蹋啦。”迷亭先生听罢说：“不错，这倒的确是有点与众不同哩。”这么一来，引起了迷亭先生更大的兴趣，把吸到肚里的云井牌烟又喷到鼻孔，烟在中途一时找不到出路，呛在喉咙的地方。这位老兄手里握着烟袋杆儿“吭”、“吭”地咳嗽起来。主人也笑着说道：“前几天他来的时候说，在朗读会上他担当了船老大的角色，让女学生们给笑话了一番哩。”迷亭抡起烟袋敲着膝头说：“嗯，你看，你看，多么有意思！”我感到挨紧他危险，赶快离开了一点。迷亭接着说：“就是那个朗读会，前几天我请他吃‘橡面坊’的时候，他也向我提过哩。
